The earliest life stages of Chasmistes cujus begin with the fertilisation of demersal, adhesive eggs that adhere to gravel substrates in the upper reaches of tributaries. Incubation proceeds rapidly at a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], with eclosion and emergence of the yolk-sac larva occurring approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days] after fertilisation, a duration that is consistent with the thermal dependence of embryonic development observed in other catostomid fishes. Upon hatching, the prolarva measures just a few millimetres and carries a substantial yolk reserve, resulting in a wet weight at birth of only 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. This minuscule endotrophic larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk absorption during the first days post-hatch, gradually depleting its yolk sac before the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding begins. The transition from lecithotrophic to exotrophic nutrition represents a critical period during which mortality is typically elevated, as the alevin must successfully detect and capture small zooplankton to sustain further development.

Sexual maturation in Chasmistes cujus is attained after a prolonged juvenile phase lasting several years, a pattern typical of long-lived lacustrine suckers. The mean length at puberty, derived from life-history tables for this species, falls at approximately 46.5 centimetres [Lp = approximately 46.5 centimetres] total length, representing the size at which individuals first develop functional gonads and initiate gametogenesis. This threshold body size is reached after an estimated 2,190 days since birth [tp = 2,190 days since birth], based on average growth rates inferred from scale annuli in Pyramid Lake populations at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. The relatively late onset of reproductive maturity, equivalent to roughly six years of age, likely reflects the energetic demands of achieving a sufficiently large body frame in a cold, oligotrophic lake environment. Juveniles spend their early years foraging in littoral and sublittoral zones, slowly accumulating the somatic mass necessary to support the high fecundity characteristic of the species.

Adult Chasmistes cujus exhibit a remarkably large asymptotic body size for a catostomid, with the ultimate total length reaching 70 centimetres [Li = 70 centimetres], a dimension that contributes to its status as the largest freshwater fish endemic to the Lahontan basin. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight is considerable, with fully grown individuals attaining a maximum body mass of 3,493 grams [Wwi = 3,493 grams], equivalent to approximately 7.7 pounds. This substantial adult mass is attained through decades of growth in the productive yet seasonally variable waters of Pyramid Lake, where individuals exploit abundant zooplankton and benthic invertebrate prey. The species exhibits indeterminate growth, though the rate of length increase slows appreciably after sexual maturity as energetic resources are increasingly diverted toward reproduction. Body condition fluctuates noticeably across the annual cycle, with gravid females carrying increased mass prior to the spawning run in late spring and early summer, followed by a period of post-spawning recovery.

Gravid females produce roughly 164 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = roughly 164 eggs per clutch] during each daily spawning event [F_R_i = daily spawning event] when maintained at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], resulting in an annual reproductive output of approximately 60,000 eggs. Field studies have documented that spawning occurs over gravel beds in riverine tributaries, where females release adhesive eggs that are externally fertilised by attending males. Egg and larval survival are highly dependent on suitable flow conditions and substrate quality during the incubation period.

Longevity is a defining feature of the life history of Chasmistes cujus, with maximum recorded lifespan reaching 44 years [am = 44 years] under natural conditions in Pyramid Lake at 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with delayed maturation and iteroparous reproduction, places the species firmly among the slowest life-history strategists within the Catostomidae. The oldest individuals often exceed 40 years and continue to spawn annually, though fecundity may decline in very old age due to reproductive senescence. This remarkable longevity is facilitated by the cold, stable thermal environment of Pyramid Lake, which reduces metabolic expenditure and slows the accumulation of physiological damage. Such a life-history strategy is particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic disturbances, including habitat fragmentation from dam construction and water diversion, which can disrupt the specific thermal and flow conditions required for successful spawning and recruitment. Conservation efforts must therefore prioritise maintaining natural flow regimes and thermal habitats.
